newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo May M1 seen above 6.0 bln dinars - institute.
newsitem.headline: Yugo May M1 seen above 6.0 bln dinars - institute.

text.p: The Yugoslav central bank monetary policy has become expansive again, with M1 growing to over six billion dinars ($1.054 billion) in May, the Belgrade-based Economics Institute said on Monday.

"The situation in May was characterised by an expansion of money supply on one hand, and a recurrence of problems in collection of public revenues on the other," said Miroljub Labus, a leading economist with the institute.

According to Labus, this shows the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) has again resorted to expansive monetary policy, which could be a possible indicator of a future crisis in collection of public revenues.
"My estimate is that M1 has grown substantially in May and is now certainly over six billion dinars, so the limit from December last year has long been surpassed," Labus said.

A monetary expansion in the last days of 1996, when M1 rose to 5.495 billion from 5.042 billion the previous month, pushed the dinar black market exchange rate down to 4.3 dinars to the German mark, its lowest since 1994.
The central bank began withdrawing money to stabilise the market and restore financial discipline, reducing M1 to 5.235 billion in January and further to 5.157 in February.
M1 has since been rising to reach 5.562 billion in April from 5.289 in March. The central bank publishes M1 data with up to two months delay.
Labus said the recent issue of new 100 dinar notes was an obvious sign of the monetary expansion. "A new note is never put into circulation to reduce money supply."
According to Labus, cash, which accounted for 48 percent of M1 in April, was now probably around 50 percent, which is putting pressure on the exchange rate and prices.
Government sources last week denied rumours the appearance of the new 100 dinar note indicated a pending devaluation.

The dinar slid slightly on the black market over the past few days to 3.6 to the German mark after staying at 3.5 for weeks. The official exchange rate of 3.3 dinars to the mark was fixed in 1995 after a 70 percent devaluation to bring it in line with the then black market value. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom + 381 11 222 4305
